title: Frostbite: what to do and what not to do
asks: my fingers are white and numb from the cold what do i do
how warm should the water be to thaw frostbite
frostbitten feet do i thaw them or keep walking
can i warm frostbite by the fire
frostbite on both feet, two days from the trailhead, thaw or not, over
answer: Get the person out of the cold and wind into a warm, sheltered place.
Suspect hypothermia and treat it first: preventing hypothermia is more important than rewarming the frostbite quickly.
Remove wet or tight clothing, and remove jewelry from the frostbitten area.
Do not thaw the part if it could freeze again (for example during evacuation). Once thawed, tissue must not refreeze.
Deep frostbite: no feeling at all, the part feels wooden or hard, and the skin does not move over the tissue underneath or rebound when dented.
If medical care can be reached in 1 to 2 hours and the frostbite is deep: delaying treatment until then carries less risk than improper rewarming or refreezing.

If care is more than 2 hours away, sources differ for deep frostbite. The Army cold-injury bulletin gives field treatment: rewarm in warm water, as long as the part cannot refreeze. The Army cold-weather manual says do not try to thaw deep frostbite in the field: move the person to shelter, evacuate immediately and let the physician thaw it.

To rewarm: use a warm (not hot) water bath, gently circulated, in a container large enough that the part does not touch the sides or bottom, until the area is soft and pliable to the touch (about 30 minutes).

Water temperature: sources differ. The Army cold-injury bulletin says 98-104 °F (37-40 °C) in its text and 98.6-102.2 °F (37-39 °C) in its field table. The Joint Trauma System frostbite guideline says 104-108 °F (40-42 °C).
The Army cold-injury bulletin says a bath thermometer must be used to keep the water in that range. The Army first aid manual gives no temperature: it says warm (not hot) water.
If a warm water bath is not possible, let the part thaw at room temperature or against a buddy's skin (armpit or groin).
Expect severe pain during rewarming. Over-the-counter pain relievers like ibuprofen can help; the Army first aid manual says to consult a health care professional before giving any medication.
After thawing: let it air dry (do not rub), cover it with dry, bulky dressings, keep the part raised if possible, and protect it from refreezing and from injury.
Do not walk on thawed feet (unless only the tips of the toes are affected). If you must walk on a frozen foot, try to do so without thawing it.
Get medical care: frostbite requires medical evaluation and treatment, even if it looks mild.
warnings: Do not rub or massage the frostbitten area.
Do not rub it with snow or apply cold water soaks.
Never use open flames, stove tops, hot vehicle exhaust, steam or directly applied heat packs. The person may not sense the heat and could be burned.
Rewarming can expose other dangers, such as bleeding that had stopped while the tissue was frozen.
No tobacco or alcohol: tobacco narrows blood vessels and reduces blood flow to the injured area; alcohol increases the loss of body heat.

quotes.text: Move to a warm environment: Get the person out of the cold and into a warm area as soon as possible to prevent further damage. • Remove wet or constrictive clothing: Take off any wet clothing or accessories that could contribute to heat loss or restrict blood flow to the affected area.
All Soldiers with frostbite injuries should be suspected of being hypothermic.

If care can be reached in 1-2 hours, the risks of improper rewarming or refreezing outweigh the risks of delaying treatment for 3rd or 4th degree frostbite. If care will not be reached for > 2 hours, most frostbite injuries will rewarm spontaneously. Prevent and treat hypothermia above all else. During field management, it is more important to prevent hypothermia than to rewarm frostbite rapidly. Protect rewarmed area from refreezing.

Superficial frostbite is defined as no or minimal anticipated tissue loss, corresponding to 1st and 2nd degree injury, whereas deep frostbite anticipates tissue loss will occur, corresponding to 3rd and 4th degree injury.

Table 4–7 Field treatment of frostbite, greater than 2 hours from definitive care 1 Remove jewelry or other extraneous material from the body area 2 Remove wet clothing 3 Protect from wind Rapidly rewarm in water heated and maintained between 98.6-102.2 °F (37-39 °C) until area 4 becomes soft and pliable to the touch (~30 minutes); allow spontaneous or passive thawing if rapid rewarming is not possible. Place in armpit/groin of buddy for 10 minutes.

7 Air dry (do not rub at any point) 8 Protect injury from refreezing and direct trauma 9 Apply topical aloe vera cream or gel if available 10 Use dry, bulky dressings 11 Elevate the affected body part, if possible 12 Maintain hydration 13 Avoid ambulation on thawed lower extremity (unless only distal toes are affected)

Once a tissue is thawed, it must not freeze again. If there is the possibility that tissue could be thawed and then refreeze (for example, during evacuation), do not allow the tissue to be thawed, since re-formation of ice crystals will cause increased tissue damage. In addition, further trauma to frozen or injured parts should be avoided, and this includes walking on injured feet and rubbing the affected tissue. If Soldiers must walk on a frozen extremity, they should try to do so without thawing the injury.

Deep frostbite skin discoloration presents in much the same manner as superficial frostbite. There is no tactile sensation at all. The Soldier might describe it as feeling wooden. Skin does not move over the underlying tissue and when dented, does not rebound. Skin can also feel hard to the touch.

When deep frostbite does occur, the Soldier should be moved to a sheltered area and evacuated to a medical treatment facility immediately. If possible, do not allow the victim to walk if the feet are frozen, and avoid treating or thawing the affected area. Thawing deep frostbite in the field increases pain and invites infection, greater damage, and possibly gangrene. Do not try to thaw deep frostbite; let the physician do it.

If the decision is made to rewarm the frostbite injury, a warm water bath with temperature of 98-104 °F (37-40 °C) should be prepared. A container must be available that is large enough to accommodate the frostbitten tissue without the tissue touching the sides or bottom of the container. (It is important that hot water not be used because the local heat dissipation procedures are impaired, and tissue injury could result.) A bath thermometer that reads in the range of 98-104 °F (37-40 °C) must be used. The water needs to be gently circulated around the affected tissue between these temperature ranges.
Patients with diagnosis of frostbite have rewarming of affected extremities with 104-108°F (40-42°C) water.
The temperature is important, as there is reduced effect with cooler temperatures and higher temperatures will cause burns.

Gradually rewarm the affected area: Immerse the frostbit area in warm (not hot) water or use warm compresses. Avoid using direct heat sources like fires or heating pads, as the person may not be able to sense heat properly and could burn the skin. • Avoid rubbing or massaging the area: Vigorous rubbing can further damage the tissues. Let the affected area rewarm naturally. • Protect and elevate the affected area: Once the frostbitten area has thawed, cover it with a sterile dressing or clean cloth. Keep the area elevated to reduce swelling, if possible.
Frostbite can be thawed at room temperature or against a buddy’s skin.
The re-warming process can be expected to be very painful and narcotic and non-steroidal medications, including Ibuprofen/Aspirin and/or Ketamine should be utilized liberally.

Offer pain relief if needed: Over-the-counter pain relievers like ibuprofen can help alleviate pain and reduce inflammation. However, consult a health care professional before administering any medication. • Seek medical attention: Frostbite requires medical evaluation and treatment. Even if the frostbite appears mild, professional medical care is essential to assess the extent of the injury and prevent complications.
Rubbing the affected areas is to be avoided as this will further traumatize the skin.
Do not rub the frostbitten area with snow or apply cold water soaks. • Do not rewarm the affected area by massaging or exposing it to open fire.

For rewarming, avoid exposure to excessive heat, mechanical trauma (for example, rubbing affected tissue), or any factor causing a circulation loss. External heat using open flames, stovetops, hot air from vehicle exhaust, steam, or directly applied heat packs should never be used.

Rewarming could also expose other life-threatening factors such as blood loss, which initially stopped when the tissue became frozen. Other considerations include treating open blisters, which are susceptible to infection and should be covered by sterile bandages and treated with a topical antibiotic. Soldiers should not use tobacco products, which can cause vasoconstriction and decrease blood flow to the injured area.
Do not allow the victim to use alcohol or tobacco: • Alcohol increases the loss of body heat. • Tobacco causes blood vessels to narrow in the arms and legs.

conflict: (1) Thawing deep frostbite far from care: TB MED 508 (2026) Table 4-7 gives field treatment when more than 2 hours from definitive care, including rapid rewarming in water; TC 21-3 (2025) says 'Do not try to thaw deep frostbite; let the physician do it' and to evacuate immediately; ATP 4-25.12 (2014, change 2 of 2025) says the injury can be rewarmed in the field but also 'do not thaw frozen areas if treatment will be delayed'; the JTS Frostbite CPG (2017) allows rapid rewarming at the point of initial care if there is no risk of refreezing. The card shows the TB MED 508 and TC 21-3 positions side by side; the owner must choose. (2) Water temperature: TB MED 508 says 98-104 F (37-40 C) in para 4-7g, 98.6-102.2 F (37-39 C) in Table 4-7 and 100-104 F in appendix B; the JTS Frostbite CPG says 104-108 F (40-42 C) for 15-30 minutes; ATP 3-50.21 (2018) says 99-109 F (37-43 C); ATP 4-02.11 (2026) says only 'warm (not hot) water'. The card shows the TB MED 508 and JTS ranges; the owner must choose. (3) Speed: ATP 4-02.11 says 'Gradually rewarm'; TB MED 508 says 'Rapidly rewarm' and JTS says tissue survival is better with rapid rewarming; JTS also calls passive rewarming 'not considered acceptable, but may be the only option', while TB MED 508 allows thawing at room temperature or against a buddy's skin. The card avoids both adverbs. (4) Ibuprofen dose: TB MED 508 gives 12 mg/kg/day divided twice daily; JTS gives 400 mg every 6 hours; ATP 4-02.11 says to consult a health care professional first. The card gives no dose. (5) TC 21-3 and ATP 3-50.21 list exercise to improve circulation; TB MED 508 says to avoid walking on thawed feet and other mechanical trauma. Exercise is not in the card. (6) Thermometer: TB MED 508 says a bath thermometer 'must be used'; ATP 4-02.11 gives no temperature, only 'warm (not hot) water'; the card states both and adds no fallback rule of its own. HHS Ship's Medicine Chest (2003) and FEMA P-2064 (2020) were searched: neither covers frostbite treatment.
